rgb: The scene is an indoor floor workspace viewed directly downward from the camera wearer, who is kneeling on a floor partly covered with dark wood-grain laminate planks over a dark speckled underlayment, bordered by white walls and a doorway. The camera wearer's own torso, knees, and outstretched arms are in the lower foreground, with their hands resting on the floor about 3 to 5 metres below the head-mounted camera and spaced roughly 3 to 5 metres apart. In the first three frames, the wearer faces away from a white wall corner directly ahead (about 3 to 5 metres away) with a metal putty knife lying on the planks between and slightly ahead of their hands, out of arm's reach at roughly 3 to 5 metres from the camera. Between frames 2 and 5, the camera wearer rotates counter-clockwise by roughly 90 degrees and shifts forward/leftward onto the unplanked underlayment section while repositioning their hands farther from their knees along the exposed plank edges. By frame 5, the putty knife lies further to the right (about 3 to 5 metres away), a red-and-black tool and a hand tool rest on the underlayment to the far left (about 3 to 5 metres away), and a second person's hand and lower leg appear partially in view at the top left edge, roughly 3 to 5 metres in front of the wearer. Most of the second person's body, the upper walls, and the surrounding room are outside the downward-angled field of view, while the wearer's torso and arms partially occlude the floor directly beneath them.
depth: The depth map shows a top-down egocentric view where the camera wearer looks straight down at a floor corner bounded by walls on the upper-right and a cabinet on the lower-right (3–5 m away), with the wearer's own torso, knees, and outstretched arms in the foreground (3–5 m) resting on floor planks and subfloor (3–5 m) that lie out of arm's reach alongside a metal scraper (3–5 m, about 3–5 m between the two hands). Across frames 1 to 3 the wearer shifts slightly left and pushes both hands farther from the torso, then rotates roughly 90 degrees clockwise in frame 4—bringing the bright white chest and bent knees (3–5 m) prominently into the lower foreground—before leaning lower in frame 5 as a second person's hand and leg appear at the top-left edge (3–5 m away, facing the wearer rather than the floor). The wearer's arms, knees, and torso occlude the underlying planks while the wearer's head and almost all of the second person remain out of view beyond the frame edges. Compared to RGB alone, the depth gradients clearly separate the elevated vertical wall planes and the wearer's raised limbs and knees from the flat horizontal floor beneath them, and weakly outline the scraper's relief in frame 3. However, the map is unreliable where per-frame auto-scaling inverts relative brightness—making the floor in frame 2 look much darker and nearer than in frame 1 despite similar distance—and in frame 5 where the scraper and small tools on the left vanish completely into the dark floor gradient.
segmentation: The segmentation map labels only regions belonging to the 'person' class in the foreground (3–5 m) and at the top-left edge of frame 5 (3–5 m), leaving the surrounding walls, cabinet, floor planks, subfloor, and hand tools completely unsegmented in black despite their being 3–5 m away and out of the wearer's arm's reach. In frames 1 to 3, the wearer's right arm (right, 3–5 m), left arm (left, 3–5 m, 3–5 m from the right arm), and lower torso/knees (bottom center, 3–5 m) are visible and shift downward and leftward before rotating clockwise in frame 4, where the torso and knees expand across the bottom foreground and partially occlude the floor below. In frame 5, as the wearer leans forward slightly, a yellow/green mask at the top-left edge highlights the newly entered hand and leg of a second person (3–5 m away and 3–5 m ahead of the wearer's left hand, mostly out of view above the frame and oriented toward the camera wearer rather than toward the floor), which is harder to spot immediately against the wood and subfloor in RGB alone. However, the instance segmentation is highly unreliable because it fragments the camera wearer's single body into two or three separate 'person' instances (cyan, pink, and brown) that swap colors across frames, and in frame 4 it falsely merges a large patch of wood flooring between the arms into the brown 'person' mask.
pose: The pose map renders only 2D magenta hand skeletons for the camera wearer's right and left hands (3–5 m from the camera and 3–5 m apart from each other) against an entirely black background, omitting all scene geometry, floor tools, and yellow body skeletons. Across frames 1 to 3, both hands stay palms-down out of arm's reach on the floor planks while shifting from the upper-right/center toward the lower-center as the wearer moves forward and turns slightly left relative to the corner. In frame 4, as the wearer turns clockwise and leans backward, both hands move away from the top edge of the frame (3–5 m away, narrowed to 3–5 m apart) on either side of the knees, and in frame 5 they extend to the lower half of the image (3–5 m away, 3–5 m apart) on the planks and subfloor. This map makes the exact finger articulation, thumb-to-index spread, and wrist orientation of the wearer's two hands much clearer than the RGB image alone. However, it is unreliable for broader spatial understanding because it fails to detect the wearer's visible arms, shoulders, and knees (which are partially self-occluded and truncated by the bottom frame boundary) and completely misses the second person's visible hand at the top-left edge of frame 5 (3–5 m away, out of reach of the upper floor planks and tools).
